sections.html:
• Name: Fighting conch snail (other names: conch snail, Florida fighting conch)
  • Scientific name: Strombus alatus
  • Minimum tank size: 90 litres
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Water type: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivorous / herbivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 10 years
  • Colour: dark reddish to brown

Different types of conch snails are found throughout the world in tropical climates. Two types are called "Fighting" conchs: Strombus alatus is the Florida Fighting Conch, found on the eastern coast of the United States from North Carolina to Florida, and Strombus pugilis is the West Indian Fighting Conch, found in the Atlantic Ocean near Bermuda, in the Caribbean Sea and further south to Brazil.

Conch snails are usually found in shallow waters and often frequent reefs. They often go deeper in search of food as they age, returning to the shallows only to lay eggs. In the wild, Fighting conch snails inhabit seagrass beds, shallow reefs, sand and rubble.

A small Fighting Conch snail is an excellent addition to the clean-up crew of a 90-litre tank, especially a well-established one, where enough algae and bacteria are present and produced in the substrate to support the snail as it grows to full size. Larger conch snails need a larger tank: the more space, the better.

Their hardy nature makes Fighting Conch snails easy to care for, so both veterans and beginners can enjoy them. The tank must be set up correctly and properly cycled so that the appropriate bacteria convert harmful compounds into less harmful ones.

Fighting Conch snails should be kept in marine aquariums with sand or silt substrate that they can dig into. They may disappear entirely for days as they eat bacteria, algae and microflora in the substrate. Ideally the substrate should be deep enough for them to burrow and disappear. They are an excellent alternative to sand-sifting gobies, and do not create a sandstorm in the tank.

Consider adding a heater if the temperature is prone to fluctuating, as these snails are hardy but need stable conditions.

Salinity should be kept between 1.023–1.026 specific gravity, measured with a hydrometer. pH should be 8.1–8.4. They need hard water with lots of calcium to maintain and grow a healthy shell. Low pH can start to dissolve the calcium carbonate shells, so cracked, thin or pitted shells can be a sign of low pH as well as low calcium.

  • Calcium: 420–440 ppm
  • Alkalinity (carbonate hardness): 8–12 dKH
  • Magnesium: 1280–1350 ppm
  • Phosphates, ammonia, nitrites and nitrates: at or approaching zero before any livestock is added
  • Copper can be lethal to Fighting Conch snails

Temperature: as they come from shallow tropical and subtropical waters, the ideal range is 24–29°C.

Although omnivorous, Fighting Conch snails feed mostly on algae (that other snails would never touch), bacteria and detritus in tank environments. They happily eat hair algae, green algae and filamentous algae, and consume bacteria in the substrate as well as cyanobacteria and diatom blooms.

When eating, the snail extends its long snout with the radula, a toothed tongue that scrapes algae off surfaces.

They need a lot of food, so be prepared to supplement. They also eat food left uneaten by tank mates, and can be fed herbivore pellets (algae pellets, dried algae, etc.) if there is not enough algae growth. Calcium is vital for good shell growth.

Despite the aggressive name, Fighting Conch snails are algae and detritus eaters and are harmless to other animals. They move using their powerful foot. When not buried in the substrate or when threatened, they can appear to hop over the bottom, and when upside down they "catapult" to right themselves. They are pretty active and can be seen moving around and eating during the day.

They see motion far better than regular snails, with well-developed eyes that extend from under the lip of the shell. They also have a very long proboscis mouth resembling an elephant's trunk.

They can be kept with other fish and snails in a size-appropriate tank. They may become aggressive with another male conch, but their minor aggression (e.g. pushing) cannot harm anybody. Compatible with shrimp such as Sexy shrimp, Red Fire shrimp (Lysmata debelius), Peppermint shrimp (Lysmata wurdemanni) or Skunk Cleaner (Lysmata amboinensis), and snails such as Bumble Bee snail, Cerith snails, Astrea snails and Mexican turbo snails. Some wrasses, Coral banded shrimp and hermit crabs may take advantage of the large opening in the shell to attack them, although these snails are good at shaking them off; watch such pairings closely when they are of comparable size.

They are considered reef safe: they do not snack on corals, but may knock over some freestanding corals on the bottom.

• The easiest method is to observe a copulating pair and note their positions.
  • The most efficient way is to place them on their side and note a verge (male) or an egg groove (female) when they right themselves.
  • According to biologists, males and females can be separated in a large series by the average columella angle: 37.4° for males and 40.4° for females.

Unlike most snails, conch snails are dioecious, with females having an egg channel in the foot. A male must mate with a female and fertilize eggs before they are laid, inserting his penis beneath the female's shell. If more than one male is present, the males may fight using their proboscis. Copulation lasts from 5 minutes to 2 hours. Males can follow a chemical trail laid down in the sand by females, some as far as 5 m away. There is no trend in mating based on the size of the female and male.

In the wild they breed in shallow waters in seagrass beds or sandy habitats, typically in summer. Egg laying may follow copulation by several weeks, and multiple males may fertilize a single female's egg masses. Females can spawn and hold sperm at the same time.

Eggs are laid in long sticky streams on tank glass or rocks. They are tiny, often as small as a grain of sand. A crescent-shaped egg mass contains up to 180,000 eggs (Fighting conch: egg mass 5–8 cm long, about 76,000–182,000 eggs).

Free-swimming larvae hatch and develop into veligers, feeding on phytoplankton until they settle and metamorphose into juvenile conchs. Metamorphosis takes 18–24 days, with high mortality during this time.

In research, larvae were cultured at 20–50 veligers/L in 5-L containers, in water filtered at 5 μm, UV-treated and changed daily, without aeration, with temperature controlled in a water bath. They were fed 3000–20000 cells/mL of Tahitian Isochrysis daily. Hydrogen peroxide was used to increase the success of metamorphosis.

Conch snails are recognizable for a shell that "sounds like the ocean" when raised to the ear. The shell is slightly conical with a right-facing spiral; the edge curls outward, making it somewhat more vulnerable to predators such as hermit crabs and certain fish. Shells are usually striped.

Fighting Conch snails reach 7–10 cm. The shell is dark reddish-brown, often mottled with orange-brown or with zigzag bars of colour on the shiny parietal wall. The Florida Fighting Conch has relatively thin and pointed spines compared to other Strombus species. The two eye-stalks protrude from under the shell, and the left eye usually extends from a notch in the side of the shell.

The Strombus genus can live up to 10 years according to some studies, but kept in aquariums these conchs do not live that long.

Other conchs: the Hawkwing Conch (Strombus raninus) is a Caribbean snail with a thick, heavy shell, mostly brownish with scattered white spots and cream or white lips, growing up to 10 cm in captivity over many years. Tiger Sand Conchs (Strombus spp) are beige with darker brown bands, with a cone-shaped shell and a small crown.
